notes.title: Dev-Update 9
notes.content:
Hey everyone, it’s been a while since the last update—time to share what’s new in EQUIRE! This round of progress touches everything from showjumping mechanics to customization options and some of the bigger long-term systems like training and guest schedules.

Showjumping: More Skill, More Variety

I’ve reworked the jumping gameplay to add both realism and decision-making:

Timing minigame update: The sweetspot has shifted toward the end of the bar. You can still play it safe and hit early for a solid but average jump, or risk pushing for the sweetspot with a higher chance of overshooting into the red zone.

Obstacle differentiation: Speed now influences jumps differently. Standard jumps benefit from slowing down and adjusting your stride for height, while length based jumps, like the new water jumps demand speed to cover distance. This makes canter control unique on every parcour and introduces new risk/reward trade-offs.

[img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45011657/a1306bf742d7de1f0f7d5c3001ca33e62731e085.jpg"]

Together, these tweaks make each course feel more dynamic—your horse’s ability, condition, and your own decisions all matter more.

 

Customization & Character Updates

I also tackled some long-overdue housekeeping, updating the engine, cleaning code, and refreshing assets. But there’s more:

Character menu integration: The rider model is now part of the menu, making outfit management quick and easy.

Dual outfits: Competition and casual looks can now be set separately.

Horse equipment customization: Each horse has its own customizer for saddles, pads, and protective gear.

On top of that, I experimented with digital clothing creation and managed to put together a basic riding uniform. It’s far from professional tailoring, but it gives the characters a proper competition look.
[p align="center"][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45011657/e03c3ab89bf2a30ed194ddc7e230cd6645f9dff1.png"]

Training & Guests: Scheduling With Depth

Both training and guest systems got important upgrades this month:

Training segments: Each now consumes energy and comfort. To keep horses healthy and successful, you’ll need to balance intense sessions and competitions with recovery periods.

Guest generation: I set up randomized guest models using the same system as the player character, so each visitor now feels unique.

Expanded guest activities: There are now more activities to slot into guest schedules, and I rebalanced them so different preferences can be satisfied without making scheduling too easy.


[img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45011657/a7710384cee1ecd30efd5c4691904b796584006d.png"]

Looking ahead, I’d like to connect these systems more strongly with ranch building, for example, requiring a stage to host a talent show, or tying trail ride quality to the number of reserve areas you’ve unlocked.

 

Wrapping Up

Even though I can’t dedicate full workdays to development right now, EQUIRE is still moving forward steadily. Each of these changes makes the game feel more alive and interconnected, and I’m excited to keep building on them.

That’s all for this update—thanks for reading!

notes.title: Dev-Update 8
notes.content:
Hey guys, it’s once again time to get you up to speed on EQUIRE’s development. Over the past month, I’ve had quite a bit of time to work on the game and was able to make some big steps forward.

Competition System

I’ve implemented a new menu that shows upcoming competitions. As your in-game year progresses, different levels of competition will become available for your horses:
Beginner, Intermediate, Advanced, Professional, and Elite.

To enter higher levels, your horse and rider need to gain eligibility by placing in lower-level events. Keep in mind: entering a competition will block part of your training schedule for that month, so you’ll need to plan carefully. Your horse also needs to be in peak mental and physical condition to deliver the best results.

Before competing, you’ll be able to view your competitors and walk the parkour to get a feel for what to expect. Then, you’ll start the first round, aiming to complete it without gaining faults—such as knocking down poles or exceeding the time limit. If multiple riders finish without faults, there will be a second round to determine the winner based on time and faults.

Competitions offer Prestige and money based on placement and level. If your or your horse’s Prestige is low, performing well at a high-level event can give a big boost. On the other hand, if you’re a world-renowned rider on a million-dollar steed and fail at a beginner competition, you’ll lose a lot of Prestige and make headlines for the wrong reasons.

I’m really happy with how the progression through competitions feels so far. I’ve also made a few changes to the show-jumping gameplay to make it more fun and challenging, but I’ll cover that in more detail in the next update.

Building System: Flexibility & Customization

Most of my time this month went into improving the building system, which I want to be one of EQUIRE’s unique selling points. My goal is to give players as much creative freedom as possible in building and designing their ranches.

As a first step, I removed some placement restrictions that required foundations to be combined with surrounding walls. This allows you to build more complex structures and gives me the flexibility to add more customization options for walls and foundations in the future. Next, I tackled roof elements. At first glance, adding roofs might seem simple—but I had two specific goals that made it tricky:
[olist]
Supporting various building shapes and roof types

Allowing for open structures (like riding halls), which have no flat floor underneath and need to look good from below
[/olist]
After a lot of trial and error, I now have a working set of roof elements that let you build a wide variety of roof styles. While working on roofs, I noticed it was difficult to get a good view of your building with the old top-down camera. So I added camera rotation to Architecture Mode, making it much easier to view and place elements from different angles.

I also made progress on the ranch environment. As explained in earlier updates, you’ll take over a nature reserve, with only a small clearing available for construction. The rest is surrounded by dense forest. I’m considering letting players expand the building plot later on—it could be an interesting progression mechanic, starting with a small cozy area and gradually growing your ranch as your needs evolve.



[img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45011657/66bf9e3502d60768776b11bc70a3bfcc55f1736e.jpg"]

Polish & Presentation

Once the core building features were done, I wanted to showcase them in a video. So I began polishing things further:

I Created new UI elements

Added lots of new objects: storage bins, hay bales, lamps, rugs, windows…

Introduced a painting object on which you can change the image inside by interacting with it

I posted two videos on Instagram and TikTok:

One shows the building gameplay

The other is a render video of the finished stable

Check them out to see how building works in EQUIRE. To make the render video, I built a tool that allows me to load built ranches into the editor and film cinematic footage of real, playable builds. This tool will definitely come in handy for future videos.

That’s it for this update. I’ll now be focusing on a few housekeeping tasks before jumping into more exciting stuff. Thanks so much for your continued support—more updates coming soon!

notes.title: Dev-Update 7
notes.content:
Hey everyone,
After a long break without a full-length update, it’s finally time to get you back up to speed on EQUIRE’s development!

Let’s start with some exciting recent events. The new teaser for EQUIRE was just released, and I’m incredibly grateful for all the positive feedback I’ve received. It’s been my most successful post so far, and I’m thrilled to see so many new people discovering the game. Comparing the original announcement trailer to the recent teaser, I think the progress from the past year really shows. Your enthusiasm and passion for this project are what keep me going—especially after a stretch where I, frustratingly, couldn’t dedicate as much time to development. So, thank you!
Now, on to what’s new in the game.

Horse Coats & Genetics
Horses now have coats! And I’d love to give you a quick look into how the system behind them works. The key to coat colors is genetics. Don’t worry, this won’t turn into a biology lecture but understanding a few basics might help you breed your favorite coat colors once the game is out.
Every horse (just like every banana, by the way) carries two copies of each gene that influence their coat pattern. These can either be identical (e.g., both genes say, "bend to the right") or different (one says "right," the other says "left"). When two horses mate, each parent randomly contributes one copy of each gene to the foal, determining its coat pattern.
First, there are genes that determine the base coat color—these are called Extension and Agouti. Depending on their versions, a horse can have a black, bay, or chestnut base. Then there are dilution genes like Champagne and Cream, which modify the base color in unique ways and can even be combined. Finally, additional genes control the size and amount of white patterning on the coat. Randomized pattern generation ensures that no two horses look exactly alike.
There are already two more unique genes in the game: the grey gene causes horses to lighten and eventually turn white with age, while the Dun gene adds primitive markings to the coat. I’ve tried to keep this system as realistic as possible, while simplifying or adapting aspects that might be confusing or that science hasn’t fully figured out yet. Not all coat colors and features are implemented yet, and there’s still tweaking to be done—but I’m really proud of the foundation I’ve built.

Lighting Improvements
In a very different corner of the game, I’ve reworked how lighting works. Previously, walls and some objects didn’t fully block outdoor sunlight, which meant areas that should have been dark were oddly shiny—and that made indoor lighting feel pointless. I’ve fixed this by reworking the logic behind walls, so now those beautiful lighting effects can finally shine (pun intended).

Building & Furniture
I’ve also added a ton of new furniture—wardrobes, shelves, tables, saddle holders, and more. On top of that, I’ve overhauled the building system for walls and floors to give you even more customization options. For example, you can now use different materials on each side of a wall.
Thank you again for all your support. I can't wait to share even more progress with you soon!

notes.title: Dev-Update 6.5
notes.content:
Hey, sadly no full length Dev-Update this month, because my schedule was full with non-gamedev stuff for the last month. Happily, I have a first glimpse of the basics of the newly implemented coat system for you (work in progress). 

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45011657/c259d3a95ab286f8d5bb9b89f02450bb79d22eaa.png
The Coat is controlled by a realistic genetic system that I can later easily access when I develop breeding. Furthermore, seeded randomness allows for unlimited coat variations, so every Horse will have a coat with unique details! In the next weeks my schedule gets lighter and I look forward to expand this system and create the building video I promised in the previous Update!

notes.title: Dev-Update 6
notes.content:
Hi, I’m back with another Dev-Update. I hope you all enjoyed your holidays and got into the new year well. For EQUIRE, it was 2 divided months. I took a break from development over Christmas and New Year's and then got right back into the depth of the building system. I worked on options that might not look spectacular and were a lot of work programming but will be crucial for a smooth building process. Walls can now have set start and end structures, which is great for fence posts. Door and window frames can have different sizes, allowing for bigger wall elements and more precise placing options for doors and windows. Besides, I added a grid placement option for the top-down building mode that can be toggled at will. In the past month, you had the chance to vote for a new building preview style, and I expanded the building options by adding a menu that lets you customize objects to your liking.

This menu can be accessed in Building (First-Person) and Architecture Mode (Top-Down) and lets you switch between different variants of a given object and its materials. For example, if you are building a new box in your stable, you can open this menu to change the material of your box walls. Maybe the lower part should be made of a nice bright wood while the metal bars are green. You can switch between different combinations with the thumbnails changing to preview all possible combinations. After you pick a material combination and build your box wall, you now want to place a gate into the wall of your box. However, you don’t like how the big door limits your horse's view, so you open the menu again and select a smaller door with a bend bar structure, enabling you to greet your horse before entering. 

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45011657/8e947561032ed04ebc597ff1227b81662460d180.png
This new menu allows me to add lots of objects and options without flooding you with stuff and makes objects easy to find. As you progress through the game and increase your reputation, you will unlock new object variants and materials. If you ever want to change the materials or variant of a placed object, for example, to apply something newly unlocked, I have also added a tool that lets you reopen the menu for a placed object and change any option you like. All of this might be a little hard to imagine just by reading my chaotic thoughts, which is why I am creating some objects to build a nice stable and plan to release a video showing how building is done in EQUIRE soon. So, stay tuned!

Because programming all this building stuff can become tedious, I toyed with some horse stuff from time to time. Petting, leading, and mounting are now in the game but need some polishing. I also added options for the customizable jumps to include little walls or hedges underneath the bar. Furthermore, after a lot of tweaking with animation and physics simulation, I'm now a little happier with the behavior of the reins, and the rider moves them from side to side when you are (trying to give/giving) the appropriate signal. If your horse listens and you begin riding turns in canter, the horse now changes leads based on the turning direction to avoid counter canters. Lastly, the menu that pops up when you are switching between different gameplay modes recieved a visual overhaul. When you finally get your hands on the game, you will see this quite often.
Next up on my list are further building features, more riding improvements, and excitingly, horse coats!

notes.title: Dev-Update 5
notes.content:
December has arrived, and with it this last Dev-Update for 2024. In the past month I prepared a presentation about the game for some application that took up a lot of time but also led me to nail down some of the vaguer aspects of EQUIRE's planning. One major part that I put a lot of thought into is the setting/story of the game. From the beginning it was clear that EQUIRE wasn’t going to be a story-driven game and would be focused instead on engaging gameplay loops, simulation, and deep mechanics. However, an interesting setting is necessary to create immersion and hook the player.
EQUIRE will put you in a role that might sound familiar to a lot of you. Someone who wants to spend their time with horses, care for them, and ride them, but their life situation doesn’t allow them to live out this dream. Too much space and money would be necessary. This is where a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity presents itself. The nature conservation authority is searching for a manager for a new nature reserve on the land of a recently bankrupt oil company. You get the job and strike a deal with the authority. You can build your dream stables and open an estate for guests on part of the land as long as you invest the profits into expanding the reserve. They agree, as the horses will come in handy to traverse the protected areas and fulfill tasks in them, without disturbing nature.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45011657/e2d8ef216c6f3b888fdc55b46c5f548ddaf44e13.png
I’m really happy with this setup for the game as it ties together all gameplay aspects and the unlockable biomes. I really wanted something that isn’t the cliché “I inherited the rundown farm of my father and lead it to old glory” and I think this setting can offer a lot of player motivation and gives me inspiration for some interesting, simple tasks that can be performed in the unlocked reserve areas and reward the player. Please let me know what you think of this setting.
On the game production side, I have also made some progress. Firstly, I have introduced weather effects as well as a day and night setup. I plan to randomly generate weather based on the current time of year in the game, but I also want to create the possibility for the player to change it, because riding out in a snowstorm might not be for everyone. To see these effects in action, look out for some upcoming social media posts. Secondly, on the building side of the game, you can now create constructions with multiple floors and connect them with stairs. When building a staircase, the ground of the next floor will create a matching hole, generating the necessary headroom for the player to go up the stairs. When looking at buildings in the top-down architecture mode, you can now change the active level to hide all floors and roofs above. This means you can always go back and add larger structures like walls or rooms to the lower floors of your buildings.
Besides some smaller improvements, like a change for the look of the arena crowd, I also started to add the framework for more interaction between player and horse. I have mostly finished the initial version of a mount and dismount animation, and things like petting on and off the horse, as well as leading the horse from the ground, are things I want to tackle next.
On a larger scale, I have flirted with the thought of working towards a riding demo to get you something to play and collect some feedback on the riding mechanics. This demo would include not much more than a training arena that lets you pick a parkour and a horse to ride it with. No building or management aspects and a release off steam, because I want to publish a more complete demo there later on. I would like to hear your thoughts on the setting I proposed and the idea of this riding demo and wish you all a nice holiday season. You will hear from me again in the new year!

notes.title: Dev-Update 4
notes.content:
While gameplay mechanics and loops are often more critical than graphics, a visually appealing game can make a big difference, especially for first impressions. Over the past few months, I’ve dedicated time to enhancing EQUIRE’s core visuals to reflect the quality I envision for the finished game.
First, I upgraded the horse model itself. Alice from The Mane Quest highlighted a model she described as “the best game-ready horse model I’ve seen to date,” and her praise wasn’t misplaced—it brings a new level of realism to the game, even though there’s still room for improvement. In addition, I’ve created new English tack and refined rider animations, both of which are a big step up thanks to your feedback. I’ll showcase these improvements in greater detail soon, especially as I continue to implement more refined movement types.

Having multiple different models and a variety of breeds in the game is still something I will consider in the future and would love to have but would likely need outside financing through crowdfunding or a grant. 

Another area I’ve focused on is customization, a key element of EQUIRE. Player customization has been a strong request in feedback on other horse games, so I’ve introduced a customizable main character, replacing the previous static one. This not only gives players more self-expression but also allows for unique appearances among guests and potential staff members, enhancing immersion.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45011657/41924ccf32d6e55af848fa4bc11176d5144de6fa.png
Similarly, I’ve improved the in-game building tools to give players greater creative freedom. You can now interact with placed obstacles to adjust details like stand type, height, and bar color or pattern. In the future, I plan to add even more options, such as the ability to switch an obstacle from a vertical jump to an oxer.

As for the riding gameplay, I’ve been experimenting with different systems and mechanics to find the right balance. I want riding to be engaging and obstacles to present a satisfying challenge. Courses should be easy to understand but difficult to master, giving players room to showcase their skills. Horse stats and personality should influence gameplay in a meaningful way—enough to add depth but without reducing player agency. There’s a lot to consider in designing this core aspect of the game, and it’s still a work in progress.

notes.title: Dev-Update 3
notes.content:
Hey guys, another month, another update. Continuing down the path I laid out in the last update, implementing guests was my top priority. I started by enabling you to open and close the ranch. If it is open, guests will come to your ranch based on your ranch's reputation and limited by the amount of guest rooms and horses you have available. You can then assign specific horses to each guest and put guests in groups that share an activity schedule. It will be beneficial to group guests with similar profiles because it will make it easier for you to create a schedule that fits the guests’ preferences. The guest profile consists of age, riding experience and three stats that describe the guests preferences on a scale from 1 to 10. They are playful-competitive, calm-energetic and theorist-practicalist.

Furthermore, I took the opportunity to expand on the schedule mechanic of horse training and guest activities while working on guests. The guest activity plan works really similar to the training schedule you have already seen but consists of 6 activity slots instead of 4. These can be filled with activities for each guest group you create individually. So far, the order in which you put these activities (guest activities/training foci) into the schedule didn’t matter much, and I felt like the feature could use some more depth that makes it more fun to create the perfect schedule. This is why activities are now categorized and the order of different categories in your schedule impacts the success of the training and the satisfaction of your guests.

Training foci categories are: Physical, Recovery, Mental, Foundations and Skills
Guest activity categories are: Basic Riding, Advanced Riding, Horse Interaction, Social and Leisure (all names might change)

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45011657/e08bd31d079591add633cd191ebc6dc6503670a3.png
In general, repeating activities of the same type decreases the effect of the second one, while other combinations increase the effect of the second activity. For example, a skill training like "Jumping Basics” benefits from a Foundation focus like “Groundwork” that is scheduled before it (Image). Let me know what you think about this idea. 

I also did some first tests with guests running around the ranch and they went really promising. It was a lot of fun seeing the guests that so far only have the intelligence of the average fly trying to leave your room through a window, run around your ranch like a pile of ants and the performance hit was also fine. In the second part of the month I worked on fixing some bugs, creating a more secure backup system for my project and another secret upgrade to the games visuals that I think many of you will really like. I will talk more about this in the next update, when I’m a little further along with it.

notes.title: Dev-Update 2
notes.content:
There are bad months and there are good months. The past month has been amazing. A great video about the game has been published, the numbers on Steam and Discord are good, but most importantly, I have made a lot of progress. 
First thing on my agenda this month was a system that lets you save and load your progress in the game. This might sound trivial, but especially in a game where every player has a wildly different experience with unique ranches, horses, progress, etc. the game needs to replicate the saved game accurately every time. This means whenever you load a game the game takes the information you saved and then rebuilds your ranch piece by piece (probably a little faster than you could do it 😉). Since this is finished, the game has felt a lot more like a real game and no longer like a prototype and when designing future systems, I can easily integrate them.
Next, I created a horse market that offers new horses every month as you progress. The number and skill of horses that show up in this market will depend on the reputation of your ranch. When you start out, you can only pick from a couple of cheaper horses, but as you gain reputation through competitions, guest satisfaction, horse trade… you will get offers for more and pricier horses. When you take a look at the market, (ignore the excessive amount of gray horses 😅) you can see that not all of the information about the horses is available before you buy one. Just like in real-life you don’t know offered horses as well as your own and must make your decision on limited information. The star rating gives you only an estimate of the horse’s current ability and potential. Besides, you can see some of the accomplishments, some strengths, weaknesses and achievements. Based on these, you can decide if the price is a good deal or you’re getting ripped off 😈.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45011657/5551754df37edb5bb76e134f2590994633be3a57.png
The rest of my month was spent on fixing bugs and improving some smaller things. This made a lot of difference, and it is now much nicer to move through the many menus and switch between the different gameplay modes. I also added a part of the menu that lets you overview your ranch. This also opens after you buy a horse and lets you assign your horse to a stall. 
Next up on my list are guests. 
If you want to see the newest update and join thediscussio? You can already find another one on the EQUIRE Discord.

notes.title: Dev-Update 1
notes.content:
After we got the basics out of the way, we can now move on to the game. To start this off, I want to recap the first few months of development and give you some insights about what parts of the game have gotten most of my attention
In general, I would say that I'm still deep in the prototyping/framework-building phase of the development process. Many of the gameplay elements and systems do need quite a lot of programming before any content or depth can be added. This also means that progress at this time is less visual, and if visuals are part of the progress, they are often not final, so they won't be shared. When this changes, I will also give you some more visuals so that you can see what is being added.
So far, most of my time and energy have gone towards the building system. This is because: 1. It is the gameplay aspect that needs the most framework programming; and 2. It is the basis for many other systems I want to integrate. For example, it would make no sense to implement the guests that will be coming to your ranch if there is no ranch. The way ranches can be built and, as a result, how they are going to look play a major role in how I need to set up guests, staff, etc. This is why a lot of my work so far has focused on the player being able to switch between different building modes (top-down and first-person) and how creative freedom and gameplay balancing can be combined in the building mechanics. During the process and in the future, I had and will have to scrap many of my initial ideas. For example, I thought you could just build walls, and then my future self would figure out how the game might know where a room begins and ends. It turns out I didn't, and it's just way easier to place rooms into your buildings first and then build walls around them. These fallacies can be very frustrating and time- consuming, but they are an unavoidable part of the development process.
Other parts of the game only exist on paper so far. The open worlds and breeding are examples of systems that I have a solid plan for but haven't touched on in development. In general, I try to first answer all the hard questions I have in mind about my game before I move into the simpler development challenges and the creation of content. 
Besides building, riding has gotten most of my attention. I have gone from an initial set of horse model and animations to another, which I then modified and fixed to get my current iteration, which will probably also not be final. The riding controls are heavily inspired by real (and obviously simplified) riding techniques and optimized for the controller. You control your horse with leg and reign signals and by shifting the weight of the rider. Although a lot of tweaking will be necessary, I'm happy with the basis I have there.
To get the newest updates and participate in the question of the month, with which I recieve a lot of great feedback, come and join the Discord.

notes.title: Dev-Update 0
notes.content:
Hi, my name is Jonas, or, as you can find me here, NobleCourt. I’m the developer of the game EQUIRE which has probably brought you here. In this channel, I want to keep you up to date about the state of the game and my plans. But first, let’s start with the basics: Who am I, what on earth is an EQUIRE and why am I making that?
I’m not some kind of industry professional, nor do I have a big programming background. I’m a 23-year-old student living in Germany. I got into game development about a year ago and started developing some small projects just to learn the basics. There were small prototypes about robots swinging on ropes and an American football management game that never got to the point where you could play a game, let alone actually finish a season. These projects were neither well planned well nor did I have the know-how to finish them, but what they did was teach me a whole lot about what I can and (mostly) what I can’t do.
From the moment I started game development, making a Horse Ranch game was in the back of my head. When I told my girlfriend about the stuff I was doing, she would always tell me how much she enjoyed old horse games like Horse Life and My Horse and Me 2 and how frustrated she was at times that so many horse games lacked quality and maturity. We talked more and more about what a modern Horse Ranch game could look like and what features would fit together. I love playing management games and she is a part-time Sims fanatic, so the game quickly had its three main pillars defined: ride, build and manage.
Although I have lived my whole life with horses, I wouldn’t call myself an expert. I do, however, have tons of expertise around me. Besides my girlfriend, who has owned a horse for 6 years, my mother is my best advisor. She owned horses all her life and worked on a ranch very similar to those you can build in the game for most of it. She is (as you may expect) very happy to answer all the questions about horse care, riding and the benefits of expensive horse food that her usually football-loving son has for her.
Since we started discussing ideas and I started development, the project has grown into a passion project for me and my girlfriend, who is creating the music for the game. Seeing the landscape of games in this genre, I believe there is a need for this game and a community that would really enjoy a game that is more than “Oh look, cute horse” and doesn’t treat their players like fools or wallets. This is the type of game I hope to provide and I would love to have you here for the ride.
On the EQUIRE Discord-Server you can already find an additional Dev-Update. I will make sure to post future Updates here as well.
